slides.notes:
The engineering context
CML3112, Week 3, slide 4

Explanation to give
Use a room or floor as the physical reference. Length and width are distances in metres. Multiplying them produces area in m²; multiplying by thickness produces volume in m³.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For the displayed rectangle, 5 m × 3 m = 15 m². Density connects volume to mass. Indoor temperature, energy and cooling load are different quantities and should retain their own units.

Misconception to address
The later assignment uses slab_mass(area_m2, thickness_m). Explain its two inputs before introducing density. A number without its unit can be ambiguous.

Start with numbers and values

slides.title: Start with numbers and values

concepts.meaning: A number expresses how much or how many: 3 items or 2.5 metres. Whole numbers count; decimal numbers can describe a part of a unit.
A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

slides.notes:
Start with numbers and values
CML3112, Week 3, slide 5

Explanation to give
Begin with a physical quantity: how many objects, or how much length? A number is the amount; a unit says what that amount measures. Python stores the number but does not automatically know the engineering unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Put 3 bolts beside 3 metres on the board. Both use the number 3, but adding them would make no physical sense. A length of 2.5 m is two whole metres plus half a metre.

Misconception to address
A decimal point does not supply a unit. Read the variable suffix, axis label or task definition before calculating.

On this slide
Number: A number expresses how much or how many: 3 items or 2.5 metres. Whole numbers count; decimal numbers can describe a part of a unit.
Value and unit: A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

slides.title: Words we will use

concepts.meaning: A name referring to a value. In length_m = 5, the right side is evaluated and assigned to length_m.
int represents whole numbers; float represents approximate real numbers such as 2.5; str is text in quotes; bool is True or False.

slides.notes:
Words we will use
CML3112, Week 3, slide 6

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
length_m = 4 makes length_m refer to 4. length_m = 6 replaces that association. Printing length_m now displays 6; the name does not remember a history of both values.

Misconception to address
Changing text in a notebook cell changes the instructions. The runtime value changes only when that cell executes.

On this slide

slides.title: Python values have types
slides.caption: 3.5 + 2 gives 5.5. "3.5" + "2" joins text into "3.52".
slides.notes:
Python values have types
CML3112, Week 3, slide 8

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

On this slide
Type | Example | Meaning
int | 3 | Whole number
float | 3.5 | Decimal approximation
str | "3.5" | Text in quotes
bool | True / False | Logical value
NoneType | None | No value supplied
3.5 + 2 gives 5.5. "3.5" + "2" joins text into "3.52".

Operator

slides.title: Operator

concepts.meaning: A symbol for an operation: + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies, / divides, ** raises to a power. // floors a quotient, so -5 // 2 is -3.

slides.notes:
Operator
CML3112, Week 3, slide 9

Explanation to give
Translate the familiar written arithmetic signs into keyboard characters. Addition and subtraction look familiar; multiplication uses * and division uses /. Explain each operation on two small numbers before discussing variables.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With 8 and 2: 8 + 2 is 10, 8 - 2 is 6, 8 * 2 is 16, and 8 / 2 is 4.0. Python 3 division produces a floating-point result even here.

Misconception to address
The letter x and the printed multiplication sign × are not Python's multiplication operator. Division by zero raises an error.

Read a function call before using it

slides.title: Read a function call before using it

concepts.meaning: Python already provides tools such as print, type and float. A function call asks a named tool to do its work: print(3) displays 3.
Parentheses hold the inputs to a call. Quotes make text: "3.5" is text; float("3.5") converts it to a number. # starts a comment that Python does not run.

slides.notes:
Read a function call before using it
CML3112, Week 3, slide 10

Explanation to give
A function call asks an existing tool to do a job. Read its name first, then the values between parentheses. The comma separates inputs when more than one is supplied. The returned result can become input to another call.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
In print(float("4.5")), the inner float call converts text to 4.5, then print displays it. In print("length", 4), print receives two inputs and normally separates them with a space.

Misconception to address
Parentheses used for a call differ from parentheses used only to group arithmetic. Identify the preceding function name.

On this slide
A built-in function: Python already provides tools such as print, type and float. A function call asks a named tool to do its work: print(3) displays 3.
Parentheses, quotes and comments: Parentheses hold the inputs to a call. Quotes make text: "3.5" is text; float("3.5") converts it to a number. # starts a comment that Python does not run.

Reading Python symbols
CML3112, Week 3, slide 11

Explanation to give
Separate a value-producing expression from the instruction that uses it. Evaluate the calculation first, assign it second, and display it only if a print call asks for output. Explain parentheses, quotes and the comment symbol when pointing to them.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

slides.title: Floor division remainder and powers
slides.caption: 7 contains three groups of 2 with 1 left over: 7 = 3 × 2 + 1.
slides.notes:
Floor division remainder and powers
CML3112, Week 3, slide 17

Explanation to give
Explain // as taking the floor of a quotient, % as the remainder and ** as repeated multiplication for a positive integer exponent. “Floor” means the greatest integer no larger than the quotient.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
9 = 2 × 4 + 1, so 9 // 4 is 2 and 9 % 4 is 1. 3 ** 2 is 9. For a negative example, -9 / 4 is -2.25, so -9 // 4 is -3.

Misconception to address
% does not mean percentage. To turn 60% into a fraction, use 60 / 100. Negative floor division does not simply remove the decimal digits.

On this slide
Operator | Meaning | Example and result
// | Floor the quotient | 7 // 2 gives 3
% | Remainder | 7 % 2 gives 1
** | Raise to a power | 2 ** 3 gives 8

Reading powers signs and remainders

slides.title: Reading powers signs and remainders
slides.body:
2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. The left value is the base; the right value is the exponent.

A leading minus makes a number negative: -7. Floor division rounds the quotient down: -7 / 2 is -3.5, so -7 // 2 is -4.

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.
slides.notes:
Which operation happens first
CML3112, Week 3, slide 20

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

slides.title: Assigning and updating a named value
slides.body:
count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.
slides.notes:
Assigning and updating a named value

slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

slides.title: Arithmetic that needs care
slides.body:
Parentheses run first: (2 + 4) / 2 is 3.0. Without them, division runs before addition: 2 + 4 / 2 is 4.0.

/ gives a quotient. // rounds that quotient down: 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4.

Many decimal fractions are approximate in a computer. A tolerance is an allowed difference, for example 0.01 m when checking two calculated lengths.
slides.notes:
Arithmetic that needs care
CML3112, Week 3, slide 27

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

slides.title: A condition and an if block
slides.body:
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

concepts.meaning: A list holds values in order: [2, 4, 6]. Square brackets select a position. readings[0] selects the first item, 2.

slides.notes:
List and index
CML3112, Week 4, slide 5

Explanation to give
A list is an ordered collection. Draw labelled positions 0, 1 and 2 above three values. The position is the address, not the value stored there. A list may contain repeated values.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For [2, 4, 6], position 0 contains 2 and position 2 contains 6. len returns 3. There is no position 3. append(8) adds a new final item and the count becomes 4.

Misconception to address
Square brackets create a list when enclosing values, but select an item when placed after its name. Python counts list positions from zero.

slides.title: Read list operations

concepts.meaning: readings.append(8) adds 8 to the end of the list. len(readings) counts its items. The dot selects an operation belonging to that object; parentheses call it.
readings[1:3] selects positions 1 and 2. The stop position 3 is excluded. A slice produces a new list; it does not remove items from the original.

slides.notes:
Read list operations
CML3112, Week 4, slide 7

Explanation to give
Walk through append, replacement and selection separately. append adds a new last item; values[1] = 9 replaces the item at position 1; values[1] retrieves it.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Starting with [2, 4], append(6) gives [2, 4, 6]. Assigning values[1] = 9 then gives [2, 9, 6], still three items.

Misconception to address
append changes the list and returns None. Do not write values = values.append(6), which would replace the list name with None.

On this slide
append and len: readings.append(8) adds 8 to the end of the list. len(readings) counts its items. The dot selects an operation belonging to that object; parentheses call it.
Slice: readings[1:3] selects positions 1 and 2. The stop position 3 is excluded. A slice produces a new list; it does not remove items from the original.

A loop repeats instructions

slides.title: A loop repeats instructions
slides.body:
A loop runs a block more than once. One execution of the block is called an iteration.

for takes one item at a time from a collection. Use it when each item needs the same action.

while repeats while a condition stays True. Use it when a condition controls repetition.
slides.notes:
A loop repeats instructions
CML3112, Week 4, slide 10

Explanation to give
Read for item in values as “take one value, call it item, execute the indented body, then take the next value”. The loop name temporarily refers to the current item.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For values [2, 4, 6], print(item) produces 2, then 4, then 6. With count initially zero and one increment per visit, the final count is 3.

Misconception to address
The loop variable does not refer to the whole list. A statement after the indentation ends runs after the loop, not once per item.

Read every part of a for header

slides.title: Read every part of a for header
slides.body:
In for reading in readings:, for introduces repetition, reading names the current item, and readings is the collection to visit.

in connects the current-item name to that collection. The colon begins the loop body. Four spaces mark each instruction that repeats.

reading is a name we choose; it is assigned the next item automatically. It is not the same name as readings. After the last item, execution leaves the loop.

Updating a counter inside a loop

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.
slides.notes:
Updating a counter inside a loop
CML3112, Week 4, slide 14

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

On this slide

slides.title: Accumulator

concepts.meaning: A running total. Set it to zero before the loop, add inside the loop, and read the final total afterward.

slides.notes:
Accumulator
CML3112, Week 4, slide 16

Explanation to give
An accumulator keeps the result built so far. Initialise total before the loop, add the current reading during each visit, and calculate the mean only after all readings have been counted.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For [2, 4, 6], total changes 0 to 2 to 6 to 12. The count is 3, so the mean is 12 / 3 = 4.0. sum, len, min and max report 12, 3, 2 and 6.

Misconception to address
An empty list has count zero, so dividing by its count fails. The issued task must define the empty-data behaviour; do not silently invent a reading.

continue skips the rest of the current iteration, then starts the next iteration. It does not end the whole loop.

break exits the nearest enclosing loop immediately. Execution resumes after that loop.

A tuple stores items in order. point = (2, 3) stores two coordinates; point[0] is 2. You cannot reassign point[0].

How the four collections differ
CML3112, Week 4, slide 43

Explanation to give
Compare the access rule for each collection. Lists and tuples use positions; dictionaries use keys; sets answer membership questions. Lists can change their items, while tuple positions cannot be reassigned.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For readings use an ordered list. For a record with unit and reading fields use a dictionary. For a coordinate pair use a tuple. For IDs already seen use a set.

Misconception to address
A set cannot be indexed. Dictionary keys are unique, but values may repeat. {} is an empty dictionary; set() is an empty set.

list | Position: values[0] | Repeats allowed; items change
dict | Key: record["reading"] | Keys unique; values change
tuple | Position: point[0] | Repeats allowed; positions fixed
set | Membership: "A" in seen | Distinct items; add or remove

slides.title: DataFrame and column names
slides.body:
A DataFrame is a table with named columns. campus_energy.csv contains meter_id, building, block, month, kwh and cost_ugx.

One row records a meter reading for a month. kwh measures energy and cost_ugx gives the cost in Uganda shillings.
slides.notes:
Explain each field before indexing. This file provides the observations for every calculation in the lesson.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: The supplied file
slides.body:
Extract this week’s student ZIP. Upload campus_energy.csv into Colab using the Files panel, or keep it beside the notebook locally.

The examples below read this file. Run the cells in slide order. Keep the original CSV unchanged.
slides.notes:
Uploading a notebook does not upload its data. Check the exact filename and column headings. Each cohort has its own data, so numerical results can differ.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Import and short names: import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd. pd.read_csv refers to a function in that library.

Reading a CSV: pd.read_csv("filename.csv") reads the named file into a DataFrame: a table with labelled columns and row labels. The file must exist in the working folder.

Counting dimensions: table.shape gives (number of rows, number of columns). shape is a property, so it has no parentheses.

slides.title: Ask a question about each energy reading
slides.body:
raw["kwh"] selects the energy column. Comparing it with 5000 returns one True or False per row.

True means the reading is greater than 5,000 kWh; False means it is not. Equality does not pass this strict threshold.
slides.notes: This is a practice question, not an engineering safety limit. Separate calculating the answers from selecting the rows. True and False are Boolean values, not the strings "True" and "False".

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Selecting rows with a mask: A column comparison produces one True or False per row. table[mask] keeps the True rows. & combines masks: both conditions must hold. Parenthesise each comparison.

Adding values and counting True: series.sum() adds its values. For a Boolean mask, True counts as 1 and False as 0. table.isna().sum() therefore counts missing cells separately for each column.

slides.title: Groups and labels
slides.body:
groupby("building") gathers rows with the same building label. Selecting kwh and calling sum adds their energy.

nunique counts distinct building labels. idxmax returns the label whose total is largest.
slides.notes:
The maximum is a building label, not a row number. Group totals cover the months present in the CSV.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Counting distinct labels: series.nunique() counts different recorded values, ignoring missing values by default. It counts categories rather than rows.

Label of the largest value: series.idxmax() returns the label attached to the largest value. It does not return that value. If several entries tie, it returns the first such label.

Grouping rows: table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Mean of recorded values: series.mean() adds known values and divides by their count. pandas skips missing values by default. The result has the same unit as the original column.

Several summaries at once: series.agg(["mean", "min", "max"]) applies those three named calculations and returns a labelled Series of results. min and max give the lowest and highest recorded values.

Grouping rows: table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

slides.caption: This week uses histograms, scatter plots and bar charts. The other chart types are reference examples.
slides.notes:
Choosing a chart for the question
Explanation to give
Choose the chart from the question. A bar chart compares named categories; a histogram counts numerical observations in intervals; a scatter plot compares paired numbers. Explain what one mark means.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Use bars for mean energy by building, a histogram for the distribution of individual energy readings, and scatter for energy against temperature. A histogram bar's height counts observations in a bin.

Misconception to address
Histogram bins are numerical intervals, not separate named buildings. Changing bin widths can change the visible pattern, so state the choice and inspect the data too.

slides.title: Charts and units
slides.body:
A scatter plot compares two numerical columns. A histogram counts observations in value intervals. A bar chart compares group summaries.

plt.subplots creates a Figure and plotting Axes. Use ax= to choose where pandas draws, then label each axis.
slides.notes:
The scatter uses the supplied load_pct and target. Equipment grouping is categorical. Use ten histogram bins as required by the project.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
plt.subplots() returns two objects: a figure (the whole image) and axes (the plotting area). Store them as scatter_figure and scatter_axes.

The ax= argument tells pandas where to draw: ax=scatter_axes uses that plotting area. Keep the library keyword ax unchanged.
slides.notes: Draw attention to the two sides of ax=scatter_axes. ax is a parameter name defined by pandas; scatter_axes is our descriptive Python variable. Despite the plural name, one Axes object holds one plot here. The conventional plt alias refers to matplotlib.pyplot. Each new plt.subplots() call creates a separate image and plotting area.

scatter_axes.set_ylabel("Power demand (kW)")

slides.title: What each column means
slides.body:
reading identifies one measurement. machine identifies the equipment that produced it.

load is the equipment load in percent. target is power demand, measured in kW.

ambient is the surrounding air temperature in °C. A blank cell means the value is missing.
slides.notes: These are synthetic teaching values, not measurements from an operating site. A row contains one measurement and its associated input conditions. target is a column name, not a unit. M1 and M2 are invented equipment identifiers. read_csv displays missing numeric values as NaN.

slides.title: Reading a CSV with pandas
slides.body:
import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd.

pd.read_csv(filename) reads the uploaded table. The filename is text, so it needs quotation marks.

A name stores the resulting DataFrame. print(table) displays it, and len(table) counts its rows.
slides.notes: A DataFrame is a table with named columns. The equals sign assigns a result to a name. CSV means comma-separated values. Python is case-sensitive, including the filename.

slides.title: The practice cleaning rules
slides.body:
Keep the first row for each reading identifier. Remove rows whose target is missing.

Keep load values from 0 to 100, including both limits.

After those removals, replace missing ambient values with the retained ambient median.
slides.notes: The file has seven rows: readings 1, 2, 3, 4, a repeated 1, reading 5 with no target, and reading 6 with load 120. The four retained readings have targets 10, 20, 30 and 40. These practice rules are explicit; students must read the actual test rules on test day.

slides.title: Removing duplicates and missing targets
slides.body:
drop_duplicates("reading") keeps the first occurrence of each reading identifier.

dropna(subset=["target"]) removes a row when its target is missing.

.copy() creates a separate table. We keep source unchanged for comparison.
slides.notes: The list ["target"] identifies the column to inspect for missing values. Do not remove a row just because ambient is missing: its replacement comes later. The duplicate reading 1 repeats the first row.

slides.title: The first two cleaning steps
slides.code:
raw = source.drop_duplicates("reading")
print(len(raw))
raw = raw.dropna(subset=["target"]).copy()
print(len(raw))
slides.caption: Expected row counts: 6, then 5.
explain: Remove one repeated reading.
Remove one missing target.
slides.notes:
First, seven rows become six after dropping the repeated reading 1. Then six become five after removing reading 5. source still has seven rows. raw is a new working table.

Result from the supplied example
6
5

slides.title: Selecting a valid load range
slides.body:
between(0, 100) returns True for loads from 0 to 100. Other values receive False.

.loc[mask] keeps rows marked True. A mask is a row-by-row list of yes/no decisions.

The practice row with load 120 must be removed.
slides.notes: Both limits are included by default. A missing load would also fail this check. The row labels can have gaps after filtering; they are not the reading identifiers.

slides.title: Keeping the valid loads
slides.code:
mask = raw["load"].between(0, 100)
raw = raw.loc[mask].copy()
print(raw["target"].tolist())
slides.caption: Expected retained targets: [10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0].
explain: ["load"] selects one column.
tolist displays its values as a list.
slides.notes:
Line 1 checks load for each remaining row. Line 2 retains the True rows, leaving four records. Line 3 displays their targets. All later summaries and charts use these four records.

[10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0]

slides.title: The median and missing ambient values
slides.body:
The median is the middle value after sorting the known values. Here: 20, 30, 40. Median: 30 °C.

.median() ignores missing values. .fillna(value) replaces only missing entries.

Calculate this median after removing the unwanted rows.
slides.notes: The original rejected rows include high ambient values. Using them would change the replacement. The retained reading 2 has no ambient value, so it receives 30. Assign the filled Series back to the ambient column.

slides.title: Filling the missing ambient value
slides.code:
median = raw["ambient"].median()
raw["ambient"] = raw["ambient"].fillna(median)
print(median)
print(raw["ambient"].tolist())
slides.caption: Expected: 30.0 and [20.0, 30.0, 30.0, 40.0].
explain: The median uses retained rows only.
Known ambient values stay unchanged.
slides.notes:
The median is 30. Reading 2 receives 30. The final ambient values in row order are 20, 30, 30, 40. source remains available with all seven original rows.

[20.0, 30.0, 30.0, 40.0]

slides.title: Selecting, averaging and grouping
slides.body:
raw["target"] selects one column, called a Series.

.mean() adds the known values and divides by their count.

.groupby("machine") collects rows with the same machine label before calculating a result for each machine.
slides.notes: Explain the whole-table mean by hand first: (10 + 20 + 30 + 40) / 4 = 25. For M1, (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. For M2, (30 + 40) / 2 = 35. A group mean is a separate calculation for each label.

slides.title: A cleaning function follows the same steps
slides.body:

Build a table from the input, apply the earlier cleaning rules, and return records using the helper.

slides.title: The complete practice cleaning function
slides.code:
def revision_clean(records):
    table = pd.DataFrame(records)
    table = table.drop_duplicates("reading")
    table = table.dropna(subset=["target"])
    table = table.loc[table["load"].between(0, 100)].copy()
    middle = table["ambient"].median()
    table["ambient"] = table["ambient"].fillna(middle)
    return as_records(table)
slides.caption: Returns a new list of cleaned records. It does not print the answer.
explain: The input is records, not a global CSV table.
slides.notes:
Trace seven input rows to six after removing the repeated reading, five after dropping the missing target, and four after checking load. The retained known ambient values are 20, 30 and 40. Their median is 30. Returning through as_records preserves the column names and row order.

slides.title: The gap between group means
slides.body:
The group gap is the largest group mean minus the smallest group mean.

Our machine means are 15 and 35. The gap is 35 − 15 = 20.

This differs from the individual target range: 40 − 10 = 30.
slides.notes: Emphasise the difference between a group mean and an individual record. Use group means for group_gap. Its unit is the target unit. The observed gap does not establish why the equipment differs.

table = pd.DataFrame(cleaned_records)

explain: max and min operate on group means here.
slides.notes:
The means Series contains 15 and 35. Taking their maximum and minimum produces a gap of 20. This is an observed difference in these synthetic data, not a recommendation to replace equipment.

slides.title: What a filled value can and cannot tell us
slides.body:
A median replacement is an estimate, not a recovered measurement. It can change summaries and patterns.

Keep the original data and state the replacement rule.

A pattern in synthetic practice data does not establish real equipment performance.
slides.notes: Ask which ambient reading was actually missing: reading 2. Filling it with 30 does not prove that the true temperature was 30. Keeping source lets us distinguish recorded and estimated values.

slides.title: An identifier is not a clock
slides.body:
reading and record_id identify observations. Their numbers do not tell us elapsed time.

A time trend needs an actual timestamp or a documented time sequence.

An equipment mean describes the observed sample. Investigate representative measured data before making operational decisions.
slides.notes: Reading 4 is not evidence of hour 4. An ID can be assigned during collection or import without representing time. Likewise, M2 having a higher sample mean does not prove it is faulty. Do not infer causes or safety decisions from this teaching dataset.

slides.caption: The fitted line minimises the sum of squared vertical baseline_errors.
slides.notes:
Fitting a line to observations
Explanation to give
Use the four teaching pairs to make the learned relationship visible. A one-unit input increase corresponds to a two-unit target increase in this invented dataset.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
The pairs (1,12), (2,14), (3,16), (4,18) follow target = 10 + 2 × input. For input 2.5, that line gives 15. A tree makes threshold-based group predictions instead.

Misconception to address
These perfectly patterned values explain model behaviour. They do not establish that real engineering data follows an exact line.

On this slide
The fitted line minimises the sum of squared vertical baseline_errors.

slides.title: Probabilities and thresholds
slides.body:
A probability is a model’s estimated chance of class 1. A threshold turns it into a class decision. Lowering the threshold generally raises more warnings.

classification_case.csv supplies decisions only. It has no probability column, so we cannot recompute threshold choices from this file.
slides.notes:
A threshold at 0.5 labels probabilities at least 0.5 as positive. Do not treat existing 0/1 labels as original probability estimates. Threshold selection requires held-out probability validation_predictions.

slides.title: What each column means
slides.body:
reading identifies one measurement. machine identifies the equipment that produced it.

load is the equipment load in percent. target is power demand, measured in kW.

ambient is the surrounding air temperature in °C. A blank cell means the value is missing.

import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd.

slides.title: Mean absolute error and RMSE
slides.body:
Error = actual value − predicted value. Absolute error removes the sign.

MAE is the mean absolute error. RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error.

Lower is better on the same held-out rows. Both use the target’s unit.
slides.notes: For actual [30, 40] and predicted [15, 15], errors are [15, 25]. MAE = (15 + 25)/2 = 20. Squared errors are [225, 625]. Their mean is 425, whose square root is about 20.62. Squaring penalises larger errors more strongly.

slides.body:

reset_index(drop=True) replaces those labels with 0 and 1. pd.Series(a_list) also starts at 0.

Use the same row order for actual values and validation_predictions.
slides.notes: The validation table retained original labels 2 and 3. The baseline list becomes a Series labelled 0 and 1. Resetting the actual labels lets corresponding values subtract correctly. Resetting labels cannot fix an incorrectly reordered prediction list.

slides.title: Column arithmetic / Squared error and square root

Arithmetic on columns calculates one result per row. Series align by row label. Divide only where the denominator is valid and keep actual and predicted observations paired.

error ** 2 squares each error. After averaging, ** 0.5 takes the square root. This gives root mean squared error, which penalises large errors more strongly than mean absolute error.

slides.title: Missing values and a fair model comparison

An imputer learns replacement values, such as a median, from training features only.

A pipeline applies the same learned replacement before fitting or predicting.

Compare the baseline, linear model and tree on the same validation rows. Keep final test rows separate.
slides.notes: Revise the pipeline and decision-tree examples from the previous teaching weeks. Fit SimpleImputer on the training partition only, even though it does not use target values. A tree learns splits and can overfit. Compare errors on the same rows, and follow the supplied model settings. The first linear example uses only load, which has no missing values. The following pipeline adds ambient and learns its missing-value replacement from training rows.

slides.title: A pipeline with a median imputer
slides.body:
SimpleImputer(strategy="median") learns one median per training feature.

make_pipeline(imputer, model) applies the imputer before the linear_model.

Calling fit on the pipeline learns both stages using training rows only.
slides.notes: The training ambient values are 20 and missing, so the learned ambient median is 20. The full-data median would be 30, which includes validation information. That is why filling the entire source table before splitting is wrong for model evaluation.

A regression tree divides training rows using feature thresholds and predicts a value within each resulting group.

The lecturer’s grader runs your submitted code on unseen data.

Explanation to give

Misconception to address

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.
slides.notes:
Assigning and updating a named value
CML3113, Week 3, slide 23

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

slides.title: Numbers text and conversion
slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.
slides.notes:
Numbers text and conversion
CML3113, Week 3, slide 25

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

slides.title: Arithmetic that needs care
slides.body:
Parentheses run first: (2 + 4) / 2 is 3.0. Without them, division runs before addition: 2 + 4 / 2 is 4.0.

/ gives a quotient. // rounds that quotient down: 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4.

Many decimal fractions are approximate in a computer. A tolerance is an allowed difference, for example 0.01 m when checking two calculated lengths.
slides.notes:
Arithmetic that needs care
CML3113, Week 3, slide 27

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

On this slide
Parentheses run first: (2 + 4) / 2 is 3.0. Without them, division runs before addition: 2 + 4 / 2 is 4.0.

/ gives a quotient. // rounds that quotient down: 7 // 2 is 3 and -7 // 2 is -4.

slides.title: A comparison produces a Boolean value
slides.body:
A comparison asks a yes/no question about values. Its Python result is True or False, written with capital first letters and no quotes.

30 >= 30 asks “Is 30 at least 30?” The answer is True. 28 >= 30 gives False.

True and False have type bool. "False" is text, not the Boolean value False. Conditions use Boolean results to choose what happens next.

slides.title: A condition and an if block
slides.body:
A condition is the question tested by an if statement. if reading >= 30: checks whether reading is at least 30.

The colon ends the header. The next line starts with four spaces; those spaces place it inside the block controlled by if.

If the condition is True, run the block. If it is False, skip it. The next line without those four spaces is outside the block and runs afterwards.
slides.notes:
A condition and an if block
CML3113, Week 3, slide 36

Explanation to give
Explain an if block as a gate. Python evaluates the condition once when it reaches the header. If True, it executes the indented statements; otherwise it skips them. The colon introduces the block.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For reading = 28 and a condition reading >= 30, the “warm” line is skipped. The unindented “check finished” line still runs. At 30, both lines run.

Misconception to address
Indentation is part of the program, not decoration. Moving the last print four spaces right changes which path can execute it.

Function

A variable can refer to one value: reading = 98. A collection stores several related values under one name.

Python has several collection types. Choose one according to how you need to find, change or organise its contents.
slides.notes:
One value and a collection of values
CML3113, Week 3, slide 63

Explanation to give
Compare the access rule for each collection. Lists and tuples use positions; dictionaries use keys; sets answer membership questions. Lists can change their items, while tuple positions cannot be reassigned.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For readings use an ordered list. For a record with unit and reading fields use a dictionary. For a coordinate pair use a tuple. For IDs already seen use a set.

Misconception to address
A set cannot be indexed. Dictionary keys are unique, but values may repeat. {} is an empty dictionary; set() is an empty set.

readings = [98, 105, 92] creates a list. Square brackets enclose the items; commas separate them.

An index is an item’s position. Python starts counting at zero: readings[0] is 98, readings[1] is 105, readings[2] is 92.

Three items have positions 0, 1 and 2. readings[3] raises IndexError because there is no fourth item.
slides.notes:
A list stores values in positions
CML3113, Week 3, slide 65

Explanation to give
A list is an ordered collection. Draw labelled positions 0, 1 and 2 above three values. The position is the address, not the value stored there. A list may contain repeated values.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For [2, 4, 6], position 0 contains 2 and position 2 contains 6. len returns 3. There is no position 3. append(8) adds a new final item and the count becomes 4.

Misconception to address
Square brackets create a list when enclosing values, but select an item when placed after its name. Python counts list positions from zero.

slides.title: Choosing the right collection
slides.body:
A dictionary connects a key to a value: {"reading": 98}. The colon connects them; record["reading"] finds the value by its key.

A tuple such as (2, 3) stores ordered items whose positions cannot be reassigned. A set such as {"A", "B"} stores distinct items without positions.

We use a list for today’s readings because their order matters. Week 4 develops dictionary, tuple and set operations before we use them with records.
slides.notes:
Choosing the right collection
CML3113, Week 3, slide 68

Explanation to give
Compare the access rule for each collection. Lists and tuples use positions; dictionaries use keys; sets answer membership questions. Lists can change their items, while tuple positions cannot be reassigned.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For readings use an ordered list. For a record with unit and reading fields use a dictionary. For a coordinate pair use a tuple. For IDs already seen use a set.

Misconception to address
A set cannot be indexed. Dictionary keys are unique, but values may repeat. {} is an empty dictionary; set() is an empty set.

slides.title: A method belongs to a value
slides.body:
A function is called by name: len(readings). A method is called through a value with a dot: readings.index(105).

index searches a list for a value and returns its first position. Here readings.index(105) returns 1. A missing value raises ValueError.

The parentheses contain inputs to the operation. The square brackets in readings[1] select an item; they do a different job.
slides.notes:

len(readings) counts the list. readings.index(105) searches that list and returns the first matching position. readings[1] retrieves the item at position 1.

slides.title: Selecting a largest error without loops
slides.body:
An error is measured − expected. Its sign shows the direction. abs gives its magnitude: abs(-8) is 8.

max finds the largest supplied value: max(2, 5, 8) is 8. Compare magnitudes when the task asks for the largest error by size.

Keep the original signed error as well, because the magnitude alone loses direction.
slides.notes:
Selecting a largest error without loops

Separate error direction from error size. A negative error means the reading is below the reference. abs removes the sign for size comparisons, but keep the original signed number for reporting.

max(errors) would select 5, the largest signed value, rather than the largest error by size. Match the selected position back to both original lists.

Explanation to give
A list is an ordered collection. Draw labelled positions 0, 1 and 2 above three values. The position is the address, not the value stored there. A list may contain repeated values.

slides.title: A loop repeats instructions
slides.body:
A loop runs a block more than once. One execution of the block is called an iteration.

for takes one item at a time from a collection. Use it when each item needs the same action.

while repeats while a condition stays True. Use it when a condition controls repetition.
slides.notes:
A loop repeats instructions

Explanation to give

The loop variable does not refer to the whole list. A statement after the indentation ends runs after the loop, not once per item.

Updating a counter inside a loop

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.
slides.notes:
Updating a counter inside a loop
CML3113, Week 4, slide 14

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

An accumulator keeps the result built so far. Initialise total before the loop, add the current reading during each visit, and calculate the mean only after all readings have been counted.

How the four collections differ
CML3113, Week 4, slide 43

Explanation to give
Compare the access rule for each collection. Lists and tuples use positions; dictionaries use keys; sets answer membership questions. Lists can change their items, while tuple positions cannot be reassigned.

For readings use an ordered list. For a record with unit and reading fields use a dictionary. For a coordinate pair use a tuple. For IDs already seen use a set.

Misconception to address
A set cannot be indexed. Dictionary keys are unique, but values may repeat. {} is an empty dictionary; set() is an empty set.

slides.title: DataFrame and column names
slides.body:
A DataFrame is a table with named columns. campus_energy.csv contains meter_id, building, block, month, kwh and cost_ugx.

One row records a meter reading for a month. kwh measures energy and cost_ugx gives the cost in Uganda shillings.
slides.notes:
Explain each field before indexing. This file provides the observations for every calculation in the lesson.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: The supplied file
slides.body:
Extract this week’s student ZIP. Upload campus_energy.csv into Colab using the Files panel, or keep it beside the notebook locally.

The examples below read this file. Run the cells in slide order. Keep the original CSV unchanged.
slides.notes:
Uploading a notebook does not upload its data. Check the exact filename and column headings. Each cohort has its own data, so numerical results can differ.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Import and short names: import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd. pd.read_csv refers to a function in that library.

Reading a CSV: pd.read_csv("filename.csv") reads the named file into a DataFrame: a table with labelled columns and row labels. The file must exist in the working folder.

Counting dimensions: table.shape gives (number of rows, number of columns). shape is a property, so it has no parentheses.
slides.notes:

Reading a CSV
pd.read_csv("filename.csv") reads the named file into a DataFrame: a table with labelled columns and row labels. The file must exist in the working folder.

Counting dimensions
table.shape gives (number of rows, number of columns). shape is a property, so it has no parentheses.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Column data types: table.dtypes reports each column’s stored type. int64 means integers, float64 means decimal numbers, and object often contains text. Numeric blanks commonly appear as NaN.

A preview of rows: table.head() returns the first five rows. It leaves the table unchanged. A preview is not the entire dataset.

slides.title: Selecting and summarising a column
slides.body:
raw["kwh"] selects the energy column as a Series. mean() averages its known values.

Square brackets select a named column. Parentheses call a method such as mean().
slides.notes:
The mean describes readings in this supplied file, not a general expected monthly use.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Reading chained operations: Read a chain from left to right. In table["target"].mean(), select the target Series first, then calculate its mean. Each step uses the previous step’s result.

Rounded display: series.round(3) returns values rounded to three decimal places. Python round(number, 3) rounds one number. Keep unrounded calculations for returned assessment answers.

Selecting columns: table["column"] returns one labelled column, a Series. table[["a", "b"]] returns a DataFrame containing those named columns in that order.

slides.title: Ask a question about each energy reading
slides.body:
raw["kwh"] selects the energy column. Comparing it with 5000 returns one True or False per row.

True means the reading is greater than 5,000 kWh; False means it is not. Equality does not pass this strict threshold.
slides.notes: This is a practice question, not an engineering safety limit. Separate calculating the answers from selecting the rows. True and False are Boolean values, not the strings "True" and "False".

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Selecting rows with a mask: A column comparison produces one True or False per row. table[mask] keeps the True rows. & combines masks: both conditions must hold. Parenthesise each comparison.

Adding values and counting True: series.sum() adds its values. For a Boolean mask, True counts as 1 and False as 0. table.isna().sum() therefore counts missing cells separately for each column.

slides.title: Groups and labels
slides.body:
groupby("building") gathers rows with the same building label. Selecting kwh and calling sum adds their energy.

nunique counts distinct building labels. idxmax returns the label whose total is largest.
slides.notes:
The maximum is a building label, not a row number. Group totals cover the months present in the CSV.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Counting distinct labels: series.nunique() counts different recorded values, ignoring missing values by default. It counts categories rather than rows.

Label of the largest value: series.idxmax() returns the label attached to the largest value. It does not return that value. If several entries tie, it returns the first such label.

Grouping rows: table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

Grouping rows
table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: A calculated energy rate
slides.body:
Cost divided by energy gives UGX per kWh. First check that the denominator is positive.

copy preserves raw. Assigning table["new_name"] adds a calculated column.
slides.notes:
A zero denominator cannot define a unit rate. Filtering here is for this rate demonstration, not an instruction to delete the original observation.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Adding or replacing a column: table["name"] = values assigns that column. An array follows row order. A Series aligns by row label, so keep labels paired with the intended observations.

Column arithmetic: Arithmetic on columns calculates one result per row. Series align by row label. Divide only where the denominator is valid and keep actual and predicted observations paired.

A separate working table: table.copy() creates a working copy. Assigning columns on this copy preserves the source table, so you can compare before and after.

slides.title: A missing value is not zero
slides.body:
NaN means a value is missing. A measured zero is still a recorded value.

isna() asks “is this cell missing?” It returns True for yes and False for no.

.sum() counts True answers: True counts as 1 and False as 0.

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Mean of recorded values: series.mean() adds known values and divides by their count. pandas skips missing values by default. The result has the same unit as the original column.

Several summaries at once: series.agg(["mean", "min", "max"]) applies those three named calculations and returns a labelled Series of results. min and max give the lowest and highest recorded values.

Grouping rows: table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

slides.title: Choosing a chart for the question
slides.caption: This week uses histograms, scatter plots and bar charts. The other chart types are reference examples.
slides.notes:
Choosing a chart for the question
Explanation to give
Choose the chart from the question. A bar chart compares named categories; a histogram counts numerical observations in intervals; a scatter plot compares paired numbers. Explain what one mark means.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Use bars for mean energy by building, a histogram for the distribution of individual energy readings, and scatter for energy against temperature. A histogram bar's height counts observations in a bin.

Misconception to address
Histogram bins are numerical intervals, not separate named buildings. Changing bin widths can change the visible pattern, so state the choice and inspect the data too.

slides.title: Charts and units
slides.body:
A scatter plot compares two numerical columns. A histogram counts observations in value intervals. A bar chart compares group summaries.

plt.subplots creates a Figure and plotting Axes. Use ax= to choose where pandas draws, then label each axis.
slides.notes:
The scatter uses the supplied load_pct and target. Equipment grouping is categorical. Use ten histogram bins as required by the project.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
plt.subplots() returns two objects: a figure (the whole image) and axes (the plotting area). Store them as scatter_figure and scatter_axes.

The ax= argument tells pandas where to draw: ax=scatter_axes uses that plotting area. Keep the library keyword ax unchanged.
slides.notes: Draw attention to the two sides of ax=scatter_axes. ax is a parameter name defined by pandas; scatter_axes is our descriptive Python variable. Despite the plural name, one Axes object holds one plot here. The conventional plt alias refers to matplotlib.pyplot. Each new plt.subplots() call creates a separate image and plotting area.

scatter_axes.set_ylabel("Crusher energy (kWh/t)")

slides.title: What each column means
slides.body:
reading identifies one measurement. machine identifies the equipment that produced it.

load is the equipment load in percent. target is specific energy, measured in kWh/t.

ambient is the surrounding air temperature in °C. A blank cell means the value is missing.
slides.notes: These are synthetic teaching values, not measurements from an operating site. A row contains one measurement and its associated input conditions. target is a column name, not a unit. M1 and M2 are invented equipment identifiers. read_csv displays missing numeric values as NaN.

slides.title: Reading a CSV with pandas
slides.body:
import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd.

pd.read_csv(filename) reads the uploaded table. The filename is text, so it needs quotation marks.

A name stores the resulting DataFrame. print(table) displays it, and len(table) counts its rows.
slides.notes: A DataFrame is a table with named columns. The equals sign assigns a result to a name. CSV means comma-separated values. Python is case-sensitive, including the filename.

slides.title: The practice cleaning rules
slides.body:
Keep the first row for each reading identifier. Remove rows whose target is missing.

Keep load values from 0 to 100, including both limits.

After those removals, replace missing ambient values with the retained ambient median.
slides.notes: The file has seven rows: readings 1, 2, 3, 4, a repeated 1, reading 5 with no target, and reading 6 with load 120. The four retained readings have targets 10, 20, 30 and 40. These practice rules are explicit; students must read the actual test rules on test day.

slides.title: Removing duplicates and missing targets
slides.body:
drop_duplicates("reading") keeps the first occurrence of each reading identifier.

dropna(subset=["target"]) removes a row when its target is missing.

.copy() creates a separate table. We keep source unchanged for comparison.
slides.notes: The list ["target"] identifies the column to inspect for missing values. Do not remove a row just because ambient is missing: its replacement comes later. The duplicate reading 1 repeats the first row.

slides.title: The first two cleaning steps
slides.code:
raw = source.drop_duplicates("reading")
print(len(raw))
raw = raw.dropna(subset=["target"]).copy()
print(len(raw))
slides.caption: Expected row counts: 6, then 5.
explain: Remove one repeated reading.
Remove one missing target.
slides.notes:
First, seven rows become six after dropping the repeated reading 1. Then six become five after removing reading 5. source still has seven rows. raw is a new working table.

Result from the supplied example
6
5

slides.title: Selecting a valid load range
slides.body:
between(0, 100) returns True for loads from 0 to 100. Other values receive False.

.loc[mask] keeps rows marked True. A mask is a row-by-row list of yes/no decisions.

The practice row with load 120 must be removed.
slides.notes: Both limits are included by default. A missing load would also fail this check. The row labels can have gaps after filtering; they are not the reading identifiers.

slides.title: Keeping the valid loads
slides.code:
mask = raw["load"].between(0, 100)
raw = raw.loc[mask].copy()
print(raw["target"].tolist())
slides.caption: Expected retained targets: [10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0].
explain: ["load"] selects one column.
tolist displays its values as a list.
slides.notes:
Line 1 checks load for each remaining row. Line 2 retains the True rows, leaving four records. Line 3 displays their targets. All later summaries and charts use these four records.

Result from the supplied example
[10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0]

slides.title: The median and missing ambient values
slides.body:
The median is the middle value after sorting the known values. Here: 20, 30, 40. Median: 30 °C.

.median() ignores missing values. .fillna(value) replaces only missing entries.

Calculate this median after removing the unwanted rows.
slides.notes: The original rejected rows include high ambient values. Using them would change the replacement. The retained reading 2 has no ambient value, so it receives 30. Assign the filled Series back to the ambient column.

slides.title: Filling the missing ambient value
slides.code:
median = raw["ambient"].median()
raw["ambient"] = raw["ambient"].fillna(median)
print(median)
print(raw["ambient"].tolist())
slides.caption: Expected: 30.0 and [20.0, 30.0, 30.0, 40.0].
explain: The median uses retained rows only.
Known ambient values stay unchanged.
slides.notes:
The median is 30. Reading 2 receives 30. The final ambient values in row order are 20, 30, 30, 40. source remains available with all seven original rows.

30.0
[20.0, 30.0, 30.0, 40.0]

slides.title: Selecting, averaging and grouping
slides.body:
raw["target"] selects one column, called a Series.

.mean() adds the known values and divides by their count.

.groupby("machine") collects rows with the same machine label before calculating a result for each machine.
slides.notes: Explain the whole-table mean by hand first: (10 + 20 + 30 + 40) / 4 = 25. For M1, (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. For M2, (30 + 40) / 2 = 35. A group mean is a separate calculation for each label.

overall = raw["target"].mean()
groups = raw.groupby("machine")["target"].mean()
print(overall)
print(groups)

slides.title: A cleaning function follows the same steps
slides.body:
def names the function and its input. Every indented line belongs to that function.

Build a table from the input, apply the earlier cleaning rules, and return records using the helper.

slides.title: The complete practice cleaning function
slides.code:
def revision_clean(records):
    table = pd.DataFrame(records)
    table = table.drop_duplicates("reading")
    table = table.dropna(subset=["target"])
    table = table.loc[table["load"].between(0, 100)].copy()
    middle = table["ambient"].median()
    table["ambient"] = table["ambient"].fillna(middle)
    return as_records(table)
slides.caption: Returns a new list of cleaned records. It does not print the answer.
explain: The input is records, not a global CSV table.
slides.notes:
Trace seven input rows to six after removing the repeated reading, five after dropping the missing target, and four after checking load. The retained known ambient values are 20, 30 and 40. Their median is 30. Returning through as_records preserves the column names and row order.

slides.title: The gap between group means
slides.body:
The group gap is the largest group mean minus the smallest group mean.

Our machine means are 15 and 35. The gap is 35 − 15 = 20.

slides.title: What a filled value can and cannot tell us
slides.body:
A median replacement is an estimate, not a recovered measurement. It can change summaries and patterns.

Keep the original data and state the replacement rule.

A pattern in synthetic practice data does not establish real equipment performance.
slides.notes: Ask which ambient reading was actually missing: reading 2. Filling it with 30 does not prove that the true temperature was 30. Keeping source lets us distinguish recorded and estimated values.

slides.title: An identifier is not a clock
slides.body:
reading and record_id identify observations. Their numbers do not tell us elapsed time.

A time trend needs an actual timestamp or a documented time sequence.

An equipment mean describes the observed sample. Investigate representative measured data before making operational decisions.
slides.notes: Reading 4 is not evidence of hour 4. An ID can be assigned during collection or import without representing time. Likewise, M2 having a higher sample mean does not prove it is faulty. Do not infer causes or safety decisions from this teaching dataset.

Fitting a line to observations
Explanation to give
Use the four teaching pairs to make the learned relationship visible. A one-unit input increase corresponds to a two-unit target increase in this invented dataset.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
The pairs (1,12), (2,14), (3,16), (4,18) follow target = 10 + 2 × input. For input 2.5, that line gives 15. A tree makes threshold-based group predictions instead.

Misconception to address
These perfectly patterned values explain model behaviour. They do not establish that real engineering data follows an exact line.

The fitted line minimises the sum of squared vertical baseline_errors.

slides.title: Baseline and tree comparisons
slides.body:
A mean baseline predicts the training target mean for every validation observation. A regression tree splits input space and predicts from training observations in each leaf.

Use the same training rows and validation rows for both. max_depth=4 limits tree depth and random_state=17 makes the example reproducible.
slides.notes:
Both methods answer the same target question. The baseline provides a useful comparison. Tree predictions need not extrapolate a straight line.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: A training-mean baseline / Creating a regression tree
slides.body:
DummyRegressor(strategy="mean") learns the mean training target during fit. It predicts that same value for every new row. Compare a more complex model against this simple baseline.

DecisionTreeRegressor splits inputs into regions with different predicted values. max_depth limits the number of split levels. random_state fixes random choices so the example can be repeated.

slides.title: Precision recall and cost

Precision asks how many warnings were correct. Recall asks how many real warning cases were found. Neither alone shows all mistakes. The cost is not an approved safety limit.

slides.title: Probabilities and thresholds
slides.body:
A probability is a model’s estimated chance of class 1. A threshold turns it into a class decision. Lowering the threshold generally raises more warnings.

classification_case.csv supplies decisions only. It has no probability column, so we cannot recompute threshold choices from this file.
slides.notes:
A threshold at 0.5 labels probabilities at least 0.5 as positive. Do not treat existing 0/1 labels as original probability estimates. Threshold selection requires held-out probability validation_predictions.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

Explanation to give
A parameter is learned during fit. A hyperparameter is chosen as a setting. Cross-validation repeats fitting with different held-out portions of the development data to assess choices more steadily.

Spread of fold errors: series.std(ddof=0) measures how far values spread around their mean. ddof=0 divides squared deviations by the number of values. This describes these folds, not a confidence interval.

A plausible physical story does not guarantee an improvement. Do not use the target or information that would only become available after the prediction.

slides.title: What each column means
slides.body:
reading identifies one measurement. machine identifies the equipment that produced it.

load is the equipment load in percent. target is specific energy, measured in kWh/t.

ambient is the surrounding air temperature in °C. A blank cell means the value is missing.
slides.notes: These are synthetic teaching values, not measurements from an operating site. A row contains one measurement and its associated input conditions. target is a column name, not a unit. M1 and M2 are invented equipment identifiers. read_csv displays missing numeric values as NaN.

slides.title: Mean absolute error and RMSE
slides.body:
Error = actual value − predicted value. Absolute error removes the sign.

MAE is the mean absolute error. RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error.

Lower is better on the same held-out rows. Both use the target’s unit.
slides.notes: For actual [30, 40] and predicted [15, 15], errors are [15, 25]. MAE = (15 + 25)/2 = 20. Squared errors are [225, 625]. Their mean is 425, whose square root is about 20.62. Squaring penalises larger errors more strongly.

slides.title: Matching predictions to the correct rows
slides.body:
Pandas subtracts Series by row label. A filtered table can keep old labels such as 2 and 3.

reset_index(drop=True) replaces those labels with 0 and 1. pd.Series(a_list) also starts at 0.

Use the same row order for actual values and validation_predictions.
slides.notes: The validation table retained original labels 2 and 3. The baseline list becomes a Series labelled 0 and 1. Resetting the actual labels lets corresponding values subtract correctly. Resetting labels cannot fix an incorrectly reordered prediction list.

slides.title: Column arithmetic / Squared error and square root
slides.body:
Arithmetic on columns calculates one result per row. Series align by row label. Divide only where the denominator is valid and keep actual and predicted observations paired.

error ** 2 squares each error. After averaging, ** 0.5 takes the square root. This gives root mean squared error, which penalises large errors more strongly than mean absolute error.

slides.title: Fitting and predicting with scikit-learn
slides.body:
LinearRegression learns a straight-line relationship. fit(X, y) learns from training features and targets.

predict(X_new) uses the fitted relationship on new feature_columns. It does not receive their targets.

Double brackets, [["load"]], retain a two-dimensional feature equipment_data.
slides.notes: One pair of brackets gives a Series. Double brackets provide a list of column names and keep a DataFrame, which scikit-learn expects for X. y is a one-dimensional target Series. The four practice targets follow target = load / 2 exactly, so the two validation predictions should be 30 and 40.

slides.body:

model.fit(input_table, observed_targets) learns model settings from paired rows. The two inputs must describe the same observations in the same order. Call fit before predict.

slides.title: Missing values and a fair model comparison
slides.body:
An imputer learns replacement values, such as a median, from training features only.

A pipeline applies the same learned replacement before fitting or predicting.

Compare the baseline, linear model and tree on the same validation rows. Keep final test rows separate.

slides.title: A shallow decision tree
slides.body:
A regression tree divides training rows using feature thresholds and predicts a value within each resulting group.

max_depth limits the number of levels of splits. random_state fixes the random choices for repeatability.

With these tiny training data, loads above the observed range receive the larger training target.
slides.notes: The two training loads are 20 and 40. A split near 30 separates their targets 10 and 20. Both validation loads, 60 and 80, follow the higher-load branch and receive 20. Trees do not extend a fitted straight line beyond the training range.

Explanation to give
Begin with a physical quantity: how many objects, or how much length? A number is the amount; a unit says what that amount measures. Python stores the number but does not automatically know the engineering unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Put 3 bolts beside 3 metres on the board. Both use the number 3, but adding them would make no physical sense. A length of 2.5 m is two whole metres plus half a metre.

concepts.meaning: A name referring to a value. In length_m = 5, the right side is evaluated and assigned to length_m.

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

Python values have types
CML3111, Week 3, slide 8

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

float | 3.5 | Decimal approximation

% is remainder, not percentage. To turn 75% into a fraction, calculate 75 / 100. Do not divide by zero.

slides.title: Which operation happens first
slides.body:
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.
slides.notes:
Which operation happens first
CML3111, Week 3, slide 20

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

slides.title: Numbers text and conversion
slides.body:
7 is an integer. 7.0 is a decimal-valued float. "7" is text because it is inside quotes. Both single and double quotes can enclose text.

"7" + "2" joins text into "72". To add those digits as numbers, convert each first: int("7") + int("2") gives 9.

int converts valid integer text; float converts valid decimal text. str turns a value into text. print displays a value; type reports its Python type.

A loop runs a block more than once. One execution of the block is called an iteration.

Updating a counter inside a loop

slides.title: Updating a counter inside a loop
slides.body:
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.
slides.notes:
Updating a counter inside a loop
CML3111, Week 4, slide 14

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

A set answers whether an item is present and stores each distinct item once. It has no numeric positions. Use it to remember IDs already encountered.

seen = set() creates an empty set. seen.add("A") adds an item. "A" in seen asks whether it is present.

slides.title: DataFrame and column names
slides.body:
A DataFrame is a table with named columns. campus_energy.csv contains meter_id, building, block, month, kwh and cost_ugx.

One row records a meter reading for a month. kwh measures energy and cost_ugx gives the cost in Uganda shillings.
slides.notes:
Explain each field before indexing. This file provides the observations for every calculation in the lesson.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: The supplied file
slides.body:
Extract this week’s student ZIP. Upload campus_energy.csv into Colab using the Files panel, or keep it beside the notebook locally.

The examples below read this file. Run the cells in slide order. Keep the original CSV unchanged.
slides.notes:
Uploading a notebook does not upload its data. Check the exact filename and column headings. Each cohort has its own data, so numerical results can differ.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Import and short names: import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd. pd.read_csv refers to a function in that library.

Reading a CSV: pd.read_csv("filename.csv") reads the named file into a DataFrame: a table with labelled columns and row labels. The file must exist in the working folder.

Counting dimensions: table.shape gives (number of rows, number of columns). shape is a property, so it has no parentheses.
