slides.title: Ask a question about each energy reading
slides.body:
raw["kwh"] selects the energy column. Comparing it with 5000 returns one True or False per row.

True means the reading is greater than 5,000 kWh; False means it is not. Equality does not pass this strict threshold.
slides.notes: This is a practice question, not an engineering safety limit. Separate calculating the answers from selecting the rows. True and False are Boolean values, not the strings "True" and "False".

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Selecting rows with a mask: A column comparison produces one True or False per row. table[mask] keeps the True rows. & combines masks: both conditions must hold. Parenthesise each comparison.

Adding values and counting True: series.sum() adds its values. For a Boolean mask, True counts as 1 and False as 0. table.isna().sum() therefore counts missing cells separately for each column.

slides.title: Groups and labels
slides.body:
groupby("building") gathers rows with the same building label. Selecting kwh and calling sum adds their energy.

nunique counts distinct building labels. idxmax returns the label whose total is largest.
slides.notes:
The maximum is a building label, not a row number. Group totals cover the months present in the CSV.

Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/index.html

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Counting distinct labels: series.nunique() counts different recorded values, ignoring missing values by default. It counts categories rather than rows.

Label of the largest value: series.idxmax() returns the label attached to the largest value. It does not return that value. If several entries tie, it returns the first such label.

Grouping rows: table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Adding or replacing a column: table["name"] = values assigns that column. An array follows row order. A Series aligns by row label, so keep labels paired with the intended observations.

A separate working table: table.copy() creates a working copy. Assigning columns on this copy preserves the source table, so you can compare before and after.

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Mean of recorded values: series.mean() adds known values and divides by their count. pandas skips missing values by default. The result has the same unit as the original column.

Several summaries at once: series.agg(["mean", "min", "max"]) applies those three named calculations and returns a labelled Series of results. min and max give the lowest and highest recorded values.

Grouping rows: table.groupby("label")["value"] groups the value column by matching labels. Apply mean() or sum() to calculate one result per group. Missing group labels are excluded by default.

slides.title: Choosing a chart for the question
slides.caption: This week uses histograms, scatter plots and bar charts. The other chart types are reference examples.
slides.notes:
Choosing a chart for the question
Explanation to give
Choose the chart from the question. A bar chart compares named categories; a histogram counts numerical observations in intervals; a scatter plot compares paired numbers. Explain what one mark means.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Use bars for mean energy by building, a histogram for the distribution of individual energy readings, and scatter for energy against temperature. A histogram bar's height counts observations in a bin.

Misconception to address
Histogram bins are numerical intervals, not separate named buildings. Changing bin widths can change the visible pattern, so state the choice and inspect the data too.

slides.title: What each column means
slides.body:
reading identifies one measurement. machine identifies the equipment that produced it.

load is the equipment load in percent. target is motor temperature, measured in °C.

ambient is the surrounding air temperature in °C. A blank cell means the value is missing.
slides.notes: These are synthetic teaching values, not measurements from an operating site. A row contains one measurement and its associated input conditions. target is a column name, not a unit. M1 and M2 are invented equipment identifiers. read_csv displays missing numeric values as NaN.

slides.title: Reading a CSV with pandas
slides.body:
import pandas as pd loads pandas and gives it the short name pd.

pd.read_csv(filename) reads the uploaded table. The filename is text, so it needs quotation marks.

A name stores the resulting DataFrame. print(table) displays it, and len(table) counts its rows.
slides.notes: A DataFrame is a table with named columns. The equals sign assigns a result to a name. CSV means comma-separated values. Python is case-sensitive, including the filename.

import pandas as pd
filename = "CML3111_Test1_practice.csv"
source = pd.read_csv(filename)

slides.title: The complete practice cleaning function

def revision_clean(records):
    table = pd.DataFrame(records)
    table = table.drop_duplicates("reading")
    table = table.dropna(subset=["target"])
    table = table.loc[table["load"].between(0, 100)].copy()
    middle = table["ambient"].median()
    table["ambient"] = table["ambient"].fillna(middle)
    return as_records(table)

slides.title: What a filled value can and cannot tell us
slides.body:
A median replacement is an estimate, not a recovered measurement. It can change summaries and patterns.

Keep the original data and state the replacement rule.

A pattern in synthetic practice data does not establish real equipment performance.
slides.notes: Ask which ambient reading was actually missing: reading 2. Filling it with 30 does not prove that the true temperature was 30. Keeping source lets us distinguish recorded and estimated values.

slides.title: An identifier is not a clock
slides.body:
reading and record_id identify observations. Their numbers do not tell us elapsed time.

A time trend needs an actual timestamp or a documented time sequence.

An equipment mean describes the observed sample. Investigate representative measured data before making operational decisions.
slides.notes: Reading 4 is not evidence of hour 4. An ID can be assigned during collection or import without representing time. Likewise, M2 having a higher sample mean does not prove it is faulty. Do not infer causes or safety decisions from this teaching dataset.

MAE averages absolute baseline_errors. RMSE squares errors, averages them, then takes the square root. Both have the target’s unit.

slides.title: Counting the supplied paired labels
slides.body:
actual holds the reference label. predicted holds the model decision. In this file, 1 means warning and 0 means no warning.

== compares values. & requires both conditions for each row. Parenthesise each comparison. sum counts the True validation_results.
slides.notes:
True positive: actual 1 and predicted 1. False negative: actual 1 and predicted 0. False positive: actual 0 and predicted 1. True negative: both 0. Keep the two columns paired.

slides.title: Operations for the next example
slides.body:
Selecting columns: equipment_data["column"] returns one labelled column, a Series. equipment_data[["a", "b"]] returns a DataFrame containing those named columns in that order.

Column arithmetic: Arithmetic on columns calculates one result per row. Series align by row label. Divide only where the denominator is valid and keep actual and predicted observations paired.

Adding values and counting True: series.sum() adds its values. For a Boolean mask, True counts as 1 and False as 0. equipment_data.isna().sum() therefore counts missing cells separately for each column.

Explanation to give
A parameter is learned during fit. A hyperparameter is chosen as a setting. Cross-validation repeats fitting with different held-out portions of the development data to assess choices more steadily.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

Spread of fold errors: series.std(ddof=0) measures how far values spread around their mean. ddof=0 divides squared deviations by the number of values. This describes these folds, not a confidence interval.

slides.title: A physical relationship can form a feature
slides.caption: Explain each quantity and the unit of the mean_load_by_equipment_group.
slides.notes:
A physical relationship can form a feature
Explanation to give
A derived feature is a new input calculated from known inputs. Explain its physical or operational reason and its units before presenting it to a linear_model. An interaction allows one input's effect to depend on another.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For load_pct 50 and ambient_c 30, the course interaction load_pct * ambient_c is 1500. Separately, load_pct / 100 gives the fraction 0.5. These are different derived quantities. The interaction is a hypothesis to test, not a measured law.

Misconception to address
A plausible physical story does not guarantee an improvement. Do not use the target or information that would only become available after the prediction.

On this slide
Explain each quantity and the unit of the result.

slides.title: Mean absolute error and RMSE
slides.body:
Error = actual value − predicted value. Absolute error removes the sign.

MAE is the mean absolute error. RMSE is the square root of the mean squared error.

Lower is better on the same held-out rows. Both use the target’s unit.
slides.notes: For actual [30, 40] and predicted [15, 15], errors are [15, 25]. MAE = (15 + 25)/2 = 20. Squared errors are [225, 625]. Their mean is 425, whose square root is about 20.62. Squaring penalises larger errors more strongly.

slides.body:
Pandas subtracts Series by row label. A filtered table can keep old labels such as 2 and 3.

reset_index(drop=True) replaces those labels with 0 and 1. pd.Series(a_list) also starts at 0.

Use the same row order for actual values and validation_predictions.
slides.notes: The validation table retained original labels 2 and 3. The baseline list becomes a Series labelled 0 and 1. Resetting the actual labels lets corresponding values subtract correctly. Resetting labels cannot fix an incorrectly reordered prediction list.

slides.title: Column arithmetic / Squared error and square root
slides.body:
Arithmetic on columns calculates one result per row. Series align by row label. Divide only where the denominator is valid and keep actual and predicted observations paired.

error ** 2 squares each error. After averaging, ** 0.5 takes the square root. This gives root mean squared error, which penalises large errors more strongly than mean absolute error.

slides.title: Missing values and a fair model comparison

An imputer learns replacement values, such as a median, from training features only.

The following pipeline adds ambient and learns its missing-value replacement from training rows.

slides.title: A pipeline with a median imputer

make_pipeline(imputer, model) applies the imputer before the linear_model.

Calling fit on the pipeline learns both stages using training rows only.
slides.notes: The training ambient values are 20 and missing, so the learned ambient median is 20. The full-data median would be 30, which includes validation information. That is why filling the entire source table before splitting is wrong for model evaluation.

Execution order and saved changes
CML3112, Week 2, slide 36

Explanation to give
Describe the runtime as a temporary shared workspace containing names and their current values. All code cells use that same workspace. Running a cell updates it; merely editing a cell does not.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Run readings = 12 once. Running readings = readings + 5 gives 17, then 22, then 27 on successive executions. Restart and run from the top resets to 12 and ends at 17.

Misconception to address
If the initialisation and update are in one cell, running the whole cell repeatedly gives 17 each time. Put them in separate cells when demonstrating repeated updates.
